notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes from the sources I could reach, organized by verse, with URLs cited.

---

# Psalm 106:1–24 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## General Introduction

This psalm is the first of the "Hallelujah" psalms. It is a national confession, the dark mirror of Psalm 105: where Psalm 105 remembered God's mighty deeds, Psalm 106 remembers Israel's repeated sins. Spurgeon calls it "A NATIONAL CONFESSION" and notes that its first and last two verses appear in David's song when he brought up the ark (1 Chronicles 16:34–36), making Davidic authorship likely, though many scholars think it was actually composed during the exile. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

Ellicott says the psalm is "penitential" — closely related to the long liturgical confessions of national sins enjoined in Deuteronomy 26, with the completest specimen in Nehemiah 9. It "evidently dates from the exile period." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-106.html)

---

## v. 1 — "Hallelujah! Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever."

**Traditional reading:** The psalm opens and closes with "Hallelujah" ("Praise ye the LORD"). Spurgeon says this is a song "for the assembled people," all are exhorted to join — not just choirs or quartets. The two arguments for praise are themselves praises: God's goodness and His enduring mercy (*hesed*, loyal covenant love). "Since man ceases not to be sinful, it is a great blessing that Jehovah ceases not to be merciful." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

Gill notes that the Latin translates "give thanks" as "confess unto the Lord" (*confitemini Domino*) — confess His great goodness and your own unworthiness and sins. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/106.htm)

David Guzik (Enduring Word) says the psalmist was "desperate to draw greater gratitude from himself and God's people." Maclaren is quoted: "Surely the thought of God's unspeakable goodness most appropriately precedes the psalmist's confession, for nothing so melts a heart in penitence as the remembrance of God's love." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

---

## v. 2 — "Who can describe the mighty acts of the LORD or fully proclaim His praise?"

Spurgeon: "What tongue of men or angels can duly describe the great displays of divine power? They are unutterable." The question is rhetorical — the challenge can never be accepted "except in that humble measure which can be reached by a holy life and a grateful heart." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

Gill extends the "mighty acts" beyond Egypt and the Red Sea to creation, providence, redemption by Christ, conversion of sinners, and final perseverance of the saints. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/106.htm)

Ellicott notes that the Hebrew *tehillah* ("praise") is the technical term for a liturgical hymn (*Tehillîm* is the Hebrew name for the Psalter). The psalmist asks who is worthy to sing such a hymn, and answers implicitly: the one loyal to the covenant. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-106.html)

---

## v. 3 — "Blessed are those who uphold justice, who practice righteousness at all times."

Spurgeon: "Holiness is happiness. The way of right is the way of peace." This verse stands in sad contrast to the sinful history that follows — Israel's way was "not that of judgment and righteousness, but that of folly and iniquity." The psalmist is convinced that "the servants of such a Being must be happy." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

Gill says "keep judgment" means observing God's righteous judgments on the wicked and also keeping His laws, statutes, and ordinances. "Doeth righteousness at all times" means continual faith in Christ for righteousness and performing acts of righteousness from a principle of grace — "we should never be weary of well doing." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/106.htm)

Guzik quotes Trapp: "Thanks doing is the proof of thanksgiving; and the good life of the thankful is the life of thankfulness." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

---

## v. 4 — "Remember me, O LORD, in Your favor to Your people; visit me with Your salvation."

Spurgeon calls this "a sweet prayer, at once humble and aspiring, submissive and expansive; it might be used by a dying thief or a living apostle." He explains that for God to "remember" means to stir His compassionate action, and to "visit" with salvation means to come to the one too sick to go to the Physician. "There is no salvation apart from the Lord, and he must visit us with it or we shall never obtain it. We are too sick to visit our Great Physician, and therefore he visits us." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

Gill says the "favour" is God's peculiar, everlasting love to His elect — shown in election, the gift of His Son, regeneration, and eternal salvation. "To be remembered with this is to have a view of interest in it, a comfortable sensation of it, and an application of benefits by it." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/106.htm)

Horne (quoted in Guzik) called this "the most spiritual and heavenly petition that the devoutest Christian can bring to the throne of grace." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

---

## v. 5 — "that I may see the prosperity of Your chosen ones, and rejoice in the gladness of Your nation, and give glory with Your inheritance."

Spurgeon: The psalmist wants to participate in the good things flowing to God's people through election — and also "to be a partaker in their joy for of all the nations under heaven the Lord's true people are the happiest." He also desires to "find glory where saints find it, namely, in being reproached for truth's sake." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

Gill identifies three parallel terms: "chosen" = the elect; "nation" = the holy nation, a people taken out of all nations; "inheritance" = the Lord's portion and purchased possession. The "gladness" is "a spiritual joy in the Holy Ghost; a rejoicing in Christ Jesus...a joy unspeakable, and full of glory." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/106.htm)

Ellicott notes that the tone of this verse "indicates a prospect of a speedy advent of good" and helps date the psalm to a time of anticipated restoration. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-106.html)

---

## v. 6 — "We have sinned like our fathers; we have done wrong and acted wickedly."

**Traditional reading:** This begins the long confession. Spurgeon says confession is "the readiest way to secure an answer to the prayer of verse 4." The threefold repetition (sinned, committed iniquity, done wickedly) shows sincerity and heartiness — sins of omission, commission, and rebellion are acknowledged under "distinct heads." He adds: "Men may be said to have sinned with their fathers when they imitate them, when they follow the same objects, and make their own lives to be mere continuations of the follies of their sires." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

Gill notes this threefold confession is the same pattern followed by Solomon and Daniel (1 Kings 8:47; Daniel 9). It denotes "not only the multitude of their sins, but the aggravated circumstances of them...sins against light and knowledge, grace and mercy." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/106.htm)

Steven Cole (bible.org) emphasizes that the psalmist, though godly, "identifies himself with the sins of the nation" — a pattern seen also in Ezra 9, Nehemiah 9, and Daniel 9. "So deeply is each generation involved in the sins of its time and of the past." (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-106-grace-abounding-all-our-sin)

Ellicott: "Regard must be paid to the fact that the confession includes the speaker and his generation, as well as the ancestors of the race." This reflects the exile period, when "the national conscience...was thoroughly alive to the sinfulness of idolatry." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-106.html)

---

## v. 7 — "Our fathers in Egypt did not grasp Your wonders or remember Your abundant kindness; but they rebelled by the sea, there at the Red Sea."

Spurgeon: The Israelites "saw the miraculous plagues and ignorantly wondered at them: their design of love, their deep moral and spiritual lessons... they were unable to perceive." He says a long sojourn among idolaters and cruel slavery had "blunted the perceptions of the chosen family." The failure to understand led to failure to remember: "What is not understood will soon be forgotten." "To fall out at starting was a bad sign. Those who did not begin well can hardly be expected to end well." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

Gill says the Hebrew reads "our fathers *in* Egypt" — while still there, they did not understand the plagues' true design: that they proved God's power and that He alone ought to be worshipped and trusted. He connects this to Mark 6:52 where the disciples also failed to understand. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/106.htm)

VanGemeren (quoted in Guzik): "The contrast between the loving acts (pl. of *hesed*) of the Lord and Israel's lack of responsiveness dramatizes the greatness of God's love and salvation. He delivered a people who did not respond to his love!" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

**Reformed/Baptist distinctive:** John Piper at DesiringGod uses vv. 7–8 to teach that God's ultimate motive in salvation is His own glory: "God saves them from Egypt for his glory... Yet he saved them for his name's sake that he might make known his power." Piper argues that "God's self-exaltation — his doing everything to display his glory and to win our praise — is not unloving; it is the only way that an infinitely all-glorious God can love." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/parenting-for-the-glory-of-god-part-1)

---

## v. 8 — "Yet He saved them for the sake of His name, to make His power known."

Spurgeon: "When he could find no other reason for his mercy he found it in his own glory." God's jealousy for His own name and honour "ever leads him to deeds of mercy, and hence we may well rejoice that he is a jealous God." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

Gill: God saved them "not for any worth or worthiness in them; not for their righteousness sake...but for his name's sake, because his name was called upon them...and because of his covenant." He also cites Deuteronomy 9:28 — had God not saved them, the nations would say He lacked power. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/106.htm)

Boice (quoted in Guzik): "Thus Israel's history is as much the story of God's mercy, faithfulness, and long-suffering as it is the story of Israel's faithlessness and unbelief. In fact, it is against the background of their sin that God's patience is most fully illuminated." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

---

## v. 9 — "He rebuked the Red Sea, and it dried up; He led them through the depths as through a desert."

Spurgeon: "A word did it. The sea heard his voice and obeyed. How many rebukes of God are lost upon us! Are we not more unmanageable than the ocean?" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

Gill explains that God rebuked the sea by sending a strong east wind (Exodus 14:21), and "led them through the depths" — the deep waters standing as a wall on each side. The phrase "as through the wilderness" (or "as on a plain") means God made the seabed as smooth as open, level country. Gill sees an emblem of baptism (1 Corinthians 10:1) and of the passage of God's people through this world. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/106.htm)

---

## v. 10 — "He saved them from the hand that hated them; He redeemed them from the hand of the enemy."

Spurgeon calls this "a redemption by power, and one of the most instructive types of the redemption of the Lord's people from sin and hell by the power which worketh in them." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

Gill identifies "him that hated them" as Pharaoh and his people, who hated Israel because of their increase, because of the plagues, and because they had escaped. He also notes the parallel to Christ's saving His people from sin, Satan, and the world (Luke 1:71). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/106.htm)

---

## v. 11 — "The waters covered their foes; not one of them remained."

Spurgeon draws a Gospel parallel: "In the covering of their enemies we have a type of the pardon of our sins; they are sunk as in the sea, never to rise again; and, blessed be the Lord, there is 'not one of them left.' — Not one sin of thought, or word, or deed, the blood of Jesus has covered all. 'I will cast their iniquities into the depths of the sea.'" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

Gill also sees this as an emblem of the utter destruction of all spiritual enemies by Christ, and as a foreshadowing of the final destruction of the wicked at the last day (Malachi 4:1). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/106.htm)

---

## v. 12 — "Then they believed His promises and sang His praise."

Spurgeon: "That is to say, they believed the promise when they saw it fulfilled, but not till then. This is mentioned, not to their credit, but to their shame. Those who do not believe the Lord's word till they see it performed are not believers at all." Their song was "very excellent...but sweet as it was, it was quite as short, and when it was ended they fell to murmuring." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

Gill adds the same point: "They believed on sight, but not before, as Thomas did; whereas, 'blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed' (John 20:29)." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/106.htm)

Guzik notes that Exodus 15 records their song, but "Spurgeon detected a fault even in this belief and praise." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

---

## v. 13 — "Yet they soon forgot His works and failed to wait for His counsel."

Spurgeon: "They seemed in a hurry to get the Lord's mercies out of their memories; they hasted to be ungrateful." He adds: "This is a common fault in the Lord's family to this day; we are long in learning to wait for the Lord, and upon the Lord. With him is counsel and strength, but we are vain enough to look for these to ourselves, and therefore we grievously err." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

Gill notes the Hebrew literally says "they made haste, they forgot his works" — as soon as they were out of Egypt they wanted to enter Canaan immediately and were displeased at delay. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/106.htm)

G. Campbell Morgan (quoted in Guzik): "In the hour of deliverance faith aided by sight is strong, and it is easy to sing. But directly strain and stress return, the past of God's might is forgotten, and His counsel is not sought." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

Ellicott: "They could not wait for the natural and orderly outcome of the counsel of God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-106.html)

**Methodist/Wesleyan note:** The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary identifies forgetfulness of God as "the root from which their base rebellion sprang" — it was not a passive forgetting but an impatient eagerness to rid themselves of the recollection of His deeds. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-106.html)

---

## v. 14 — "They craved intensely in the wilderness and tested God in the desert."

Spurgeon: Though God gave them "the most suitable and pleasant food," they grew "dainty and sniffed at angel's food, and must needs have flesh to eat." Their desire became "a mania with them, and, like a wild horse, carried away its rider." They tempted God in the very place where they were "absolutely dependent upon him and were everyday fed by his direct provision." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

Gill explains that "lusted exceedingly" (Hebrew: "lusted a lust," as in Numbers 11:4) was not mere natural hunger but a "voluptuous lust to gratify their appetite" — the same "lusting after evil tidings" Paul condemns in 1 Corinthians 10:6. Tempting God meant "making experiments, in trying whether the presence of God was among them or not." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/106.htm)

---

## v. 15 — "So He granted their request, but sent a wasting disease upon them."

**Traditional reading:** Spurgeon: "Prayer may be answered in anger and denied in love. That God gives a man his desire is no proof that he is the object of divine favour." He added, "If we must know scantiness, may God grant it may not be scantiness of soul: yet this is a common attendant upon worldly prosperity. When wealth grows with many a man his worldly estate is fatter, but his soul's state is leaner." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

Guzik comments: "When we allow ungodly cravings to rule our lives, God may send what we crave — and leanness into our soul as well." F. B. Meyer is quoted: "They had their desire, but their souls were starved." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

**Protestant translation difference:** The KJV reads "leanness into their soul" while the NASB/ESV render it "a wasting disease" (following Numbers 11:33–34 where many died while the quail was still in their mouths). Gill notes both interpretations: the Septuagint, Vulgate, and all Oriental versions read "fulness into their souls" (a surfeit leading to death), while Jarchi, Kimchi, and others interpret it as immediate death. Gill adds a spiritual application: "while the bodies of wicked men are fed and pampered, their souls are starved, and at last eternally lost." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/106.htm)

Maclaren (quoted in Guzik): "For whoever sets his hot desires in self-willed fashion on material good, and succeeds in securing their gratification, gains...the loss of a shrivelled spiritual nature. Full-fed flesh makes starved souls." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

Steven Cole (bible.org): "God sometimes grants our selfish requests, along with the consequences, so that we learn not to crave evil things! Be careful what you pray for!" (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-106-grace-abounding-all-our-sin)

---

## v. 16 — "In the camp they envied Moses, as well as Aaron, the holy one of the LORD."

Spurgeon: "Who can hope to escape envy when the meekest of men was subject to it? How unreasonable was this envy, for Moses was the one man in all the camp who laboured hardest and had most to bear. They should have sympathised with him; to envy him was ridiculous." Aaron is called "the saint of the Lord" by virtue of his priestly office — it is an official, not a personal designation. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-106.html)

Gill notes this refers to the rebellion of Korah recorded in Numbers 16. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/106.htm)

Derek Kidner (quoted in Guzik): "The self-righteous attacks on Moses' spiritual and temporal leadership in Numbers 16:3 and 16:13 are unmasked in the simple words, men...were jealous. Such directness is as characteristic of Scripture as are the elaborate self-justifications of men." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

---

## v. 17 — "The earth opened up and swallowed Dathan; it covered the assembly of Abiram."

Spurgeon notes that Korah is not mentioned, "for mercy was extended to his household, though he himself perished." He says the earth "could no longer bear up under the weight of these rebels and ingrates: God's patience was exhausted when they began to assail his servants, for his children are very dear to him." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

Guzik notes the reference to Numbers 16:31–33, where Dathan and Abiram were swallowed by a giant crevice. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

---

## v. 18 — "Then fire blazed through their company; flames consumed the wicked."

Spurgeon: "The Levites who were with Korah perished by fire, which was a most fitting death for those who intruded into the priesthood, and so offered strange fire. God has more than one arrow in his quiver, the fire can consume those whom the earthquake spares." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

Guzik references Numbers 16:35 which describes fire consuming the 250 men who conspired with Korah. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

---

## v. 19 — "At Horeb they made a calf and worshiped a molten image."

Spurgeon: "In the very place where they had solemnly pledged themselves to obey the Lord they broke the second, if not the first, of his commandments." The "calf" is a sarcastic diminutive — "idols are worthy of no respect, scorn is never more legitimately used than when it is poured upon all attempts to set forth the Invisible God." He then uses this to critique Ritualism and Roman Catholic symbols: "After the same fashion the Ritualists must needs set up their symbols...Spiritual worship they seem unable to apprehend." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown): Though the calf was intended to represent Jehovah under a symbol, "as this was incompatible with His nature (Exodus 20:5), they in reality gave up Him, and so were given up by Him." The "calf" is "called so in contempt. They would have made an ox or bull, but their idol turned out but a calf." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/psalms-106.html)

Guzik notes the psalmist's chronology is not strictly sequential — the golden calf incident at Horeb happened before the Korah rebellion, but the writer groups sins by increasing gravity. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

---

## v. 20 — "They exchanged their Glory for the image of a grass-eating ox."

Spurgeon: The ox image is called a "grass-eating ox" to emphasize its absurdity — "To believe that the image of a bull could be the image of God must need great credulity." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

Maclaren (quoted in Guzik): "The strange perverseness which turned away from such a radiance of glory to bow down before an idol is strikingly set forth by the figure of bartering it for an image and that of an ox that ate grass." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

JFB notes that "their glory" refers to Yahweh Himself. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/psalms-106.html)

**Paul's use in Romans 1:23:** Guzik points out that Paul quoted from the Septuagint translation of this verse in Romans 1:23, applying it to all humanity's idolatry: "It is not Israel alone that has been guilty of the sin of idolatry. This is humanity's sin in general. We too are idolaters when we put anything but God in God's place." (Boice, quoted in Guzik). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

---

## v. 21 — "They forgot God their Savior, who did great things in Egypt."

The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary describes this as the root of their sin: "They forgat God their Saviour... Had they retained in their mind the great things which God had done for them, they would have had in these things such a revelation of His character as would have precluded the committal of their offences against Him." The progression is from forgetfulness to idolatry — "The development of evil is from bad to worse, and is sometimes fearfully rapid." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-106.html)

Guzik: "Their sin was not only of idolatry and immorality, but also of plain ingratitude." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

---

## v. 22 — "wondrous works in the land of Ham, and awesome deeds by the Red Sea."

"Land of Ham" refers to Egypt (Ham being the father of Mizraim/Egypt, Genesis 10:6). Gill notes this is a poetic parallel to "Egypt" in the previous verse. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/106.htm)

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes the reference to the "miraculous plagues and miracles" in Egypt and at the Red Sea. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-106.html)

---

## v. 23 — "So He said He would destroy them—had not Moses His chosen one stood before Him in the breach to divert His wrath from destroying them."

**Traditional reading:** Spurgeon: "Like a bold warrior who defends the wall when there is an opening for the adversary and destruction is rushing in upon the city, Moses stopped the way of avenging justice with his prayers." He adds, "Mighty as was the sin of Israel to provoke vengeance, prayer was mightier in turning it away. How diligently ought we to plead with the Lord for this guilty world, and especially for his own backsliding people!" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

Matthew Poole (quoted in Guzik): "God had made a hedge or wall about them; but they had made a gap or breach in it by their sins, at which the Lord, who was now justly become their enemy, might enter to destroy them; which he had certainly done, if Moses by his prevailing intercession had not hindered him." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

VanGemeren (quoted in Guzik): "The metaphor 'stood in the breach' derives from military language, signifying the bravery of a soldier who stands in the breach of the wall, willing to give his life in warding off the enemy (cf. Ezekiel 22:30)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

Guzik notes that God told Moses, "Let Me alone, that My wrath may burn hot against them" (Exodus 32:10). God did not ask for Moses' participation — "He simply told Moses, 'Let Me alone so I can do this.' The clear impression was that if Moses did nothing, the plan would go ahead." Moses "did not fatalistically say, 'Well, whatever God will do, God will do.'" He pleaded, believing this to be God's true heart. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

**Baptist view:** The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary draws a direct typological parallel: "Even so Jesus stands as an intercessor for the sinning child of God now, Hebrews 7:25–26; 1 John 1:9; 1 John 2:1–2." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-106.html)

---

## v. 24 — "They despised the pleasant land; they did not believe His promise."

Spurgeon: The "pleasant land" (literally "a land of desire") was "the glory of all lands" — yet they despised it, "they did not think it worth the trouble of seeking and conquering; they even spoke of Egypt, the land of their bondage, as though they preferred it to the land of promise." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps106.php)

JFB explains this refers to the sin at Kadesh Barnea (Numbers 13–14). "Despised" (Deuteronomy 28:32) and "believed not his word" — meaning they believed the faithless spies rather than God's promise. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/psalms-106.html)

The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary identifies five sins in vv. 24–27: (1) Despising the choicest inheritance; (2) Disbelieving the best-attested word; (3) Murmuring against God's arrangements; (4) Disobeying God's commands; (5) Receiving deserved punishment; and (6) Entailing misery on posterity. Barnes (quoted in the commentary) notes their murmuring occurred "when they had a comfortable home; when safe; when provided for; when under the direct Divine protection and care. So men often complain; perhaps oftener when they have many comforts than when they have few." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-106.html)

Guzik also references Spurgeon's remark on their complaining: "Murmuring is a great sin and not a mere weakness; it contains within itself unbelief, pride, rebellion, and a whole host of sins. It is a home sin, and is generally practised by complainers 'in their tents,' but it is just as evil there as in the streets, and will be quite as grievous to the Lord." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/)

---

## Traditions and Differing Emphases

**Reformed/Presbyterian (Spurgeon, JFB, Boice):** Strong emphasis on God's sovereignty — He saves "for His name's sake," not for any worth in Israel. The history of Israel illustrates the doctrines of total depravity and unconditional election. Moses as intercessor prefigures Christ. The psalm demonstrates both divine sovereignty and human responsibility.

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/David Guzik):** Emphasis on the application to the believer's spiritual life — "leanness of soul" as a warning against letting cravings rule. God "visits" us with salvation (personal encounter). Moses' intercession is held up as an example of prevailing prayer. The tone is pastoral and applicatory.

**Baptist (Spurgeon, Garner-Howes):** Christ-centered typology — the Red Sea crossing as baptism (1 Corinthians 10:1–2), the destruction of enemies as pardon of sins, Moses as a type of Christ the Intercessor. Strong emphasis on the seriousness of sin and the necessity of personal confession.

**Evangelical (bible.org/Steven Cole):** The psalm teaches that "the great depths of our sin and the still greater depths of God's grace should cause us to praise Him." Emphasis on self-examination: "As we look at this list of sins, examine yourself and confess any that may be lurking in your heart." Identifies the sins as unbelief, ingratitude, rebellion, craving worldly pleasures, grumbling, and worldliness. (https://new.bible.org/seriespage/psalm-106-grace-abounding-all-our-sin)

**Methodist/Holiness (Preacher's Complete Homiletical):** Traces the progression of sin from its root (forgetfulness of God) through its expressions (lust, envy, idolatry) to its punishments. Emphasis on moral and spiritual development — "the development of evil is from bad to worse, and is sometimes fearfully rapid." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-106.html)

## Translation Notes

- **v. 15 "leanness into their soul" (KJV) vs. "wasting disease" (NASB/ESV):** The KJV follows the Hebrew literally (*râzôn*, leanness/ wasting). Modern translations interpret through the lens of Numbers 11:33–34, where the quail brought a plague. Gill notes the ancient versions (LXX, Vulgate) read "fulness" (surfeit), indicating death by overindulgence. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/106.htm)

- **v. 4 "favour" (BSB) / "favour that thou bearest unto thy people" (KJV):** The Hebrew refers to God's gracious disposition toward His covenant people. Gill connects it to electing love. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/106.htm)
